Understanding Ingress in Kubernetes: Key Concepts and Configuration

Introduction:

Ingress in Kubernetes is a vital resource for managing external access to services within a cluster. It provides a streamlined way to route HTTP and HTTPS traffic to various services based on criteria such as URL paths and hostnames. By using Ingress, you can consolidate multiple services under a single external IP address, simplifying traffic management and reducing the need for multiple LoadBalancers or NodePorts. This guide will walk you through the essential concepts of Ingress, its benefits, and how to set up an NGINX Ingress Controller to handle traffic routing effectively. You will learn about different types of Ingress rules, such as path-based and host-based routing, and how to configure SSL termination for secure connections.

This is a demonstration of how to use Kubernetes Ingress to route traffic to different services in your cluster based on different paths.

What is Ingress?

Ingress in Kubernetes is a resource that manages external access to services within a cluster, typically HTTP or HTTPS traffic. It allows you to define rules for routing traffic to different services based on URL paths, hostnames, or other criteria, without exposing multiple services to the outside world directly. Essentially, Ingress acts as a gateway that directs incoming requests to the appropriate services within the cluster.

Why Ingress?

Imagine you run multiple web applications (e.g., a blog, an e-commerce site, and an API) on the same Kubernetes cluster. Without Ingress, you’d need to expose each service with its own LoadBalancer or NodePort, which can be expensive and complex to manage. Ingress simplifies this by allowing you to route traffic to the correct service based on the URL path or hostname, all under a single external IP address.

Types of Ingress Rules:

  1. Path-Based Routing: Routes traffic to different services based on the URL path.
  • Example: If you run an e-commerce site, traffic to yourdomain.com/courses might go to the shopping service, while traffic to yourdomain.com/blogs goes to the blog service.

2. Host-Based Routing: Routes traffic based on the hostname.

  • Example: Traffic to https://exams.mycourses.com goes to your shopping service, while traffic to https://books.mycourses.com goes to your blog service.

3. SSL Termination: Handles HTTPS traffic by terminating SSL/TLS at the Ingress, meaning the Ingress manages the encryption and forwards the traffic to services as plain HTTP.

  • Example: You can secure your services with HTTPS by managing certificates at the Ingress level, offloading the complexity of SSL management from the individual services.

Types of Ingress Controllers:

Ingress controllers are implementations that fulfill the Ingress resource and manage the routing of traffic. Some popular Ingress controllers include:

  1. NGINX Ingress Controller: A popular, widely used controller that integrates well with Kubernetes and provides robust features for load balancing, SSL termination, and routing.
  2. HAProxy Ingress Controller: Known for its high performance and reliability, HAProxy is used for load balancing and can handle complex routing scenarios.
  3. Istio Ingress Gateway: Part of the Istio service mesh, it provides advanced traffic management, security, and observability features beyond standard Ingress controllers.
  4. Contour: A Kubernetes-native ingress controller that uses Envoy as the data plane, known for its fast performance and dynamic configuration.
  5. Citrix Ingress Controller: Offers enterprise-grade load balancing and security features, with integration into Citrix ADC.
  6. Apache APISIX Ingress Controller: An open-source API Gateway that also functions as an ingress controller, offering rich plugins and high performance.

How It Works?

1. User Request

  • A user tries to access a service within the Kubernetes cluster by entering a URL, like http://mycourses.com, in their web browser.

2. DNS Resolution

  • The URL is resolved to an external IP address associated with the Ingress Controller. This is usually handled by DNS.

3. Ingress Controller

  • The Ingress Controller is a component running within the Kubernetes cluster. It monitors the Ingress resources and manages the routing rules for incoming traffic.
  • Upon receiving the request, the Ingress Controller evaluates the URL against the Ingress rules defined in the Ingress Resource.

4. Ingress Resource

  • The Ingress Resource is a YAML configuration file that defines the routing rules for different paths and hosts.
  • It specifies how requests should be directed to the appropriate services within the cluster. For example, it might route http://mycourses.com/exam to the "shop" service and http://mycourses.com/blogs to the "blog" service.

5. Routing Traffic to Services

  • The Ingress Controller forwards the request to the appropriate service based on the rules defined in the Ingress Resource.
  • The service then routes the request to the correct pod(s) running the application within the cluster.

6. Service Response

  • The service processes the request and returns the response to the Ingress Controller.

7. Response to the User

  • Finally, the Ingress Controller sends the response back to the user, displaying the requested content in their web browser.

Summary:

  • Ingress Controller: Acts as a gateway that processes external requests and directs them to the appropriate services based on Ingress rules.
  • Ingress Resource: Defines how traffic should be routed to services within the cluster.
  • Service: Handles the actual application logic and responds to the user request.
  • Pods: The units of the application that are managed by the services and run inside the cluster.

This setup allows multiple services to be exposed via a single external IP address, simplifying the management of traffic to various applications running within a Kubernetes cluster.

Install nginx-ingress controller :

To get started, you will need to install the nginx-ingress controller in your Kubernetes cluster by running the following command:

kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/main/deploy/static/provider/kind/deploy.yaml

This will deploy the nginx-ingress controller as a Deployment in your cluster.

kubectl get ns
kubectl get all -n ingress-nginx

Create Deployments

Next, you will need to create some sample Deployments to route traffic to. Run the following commands to create the Deployments:

kubectl create deploy sample-1 --image=devopsprosamples/next-path-sample-1
kubectl create deploy sample-2 --image=devopsprosamples/next-path-sample-2
kubectl create deploy sample-3 --image=devopsprosamples/next-sample-1
kubectl create deploy sample-4 --image=devopsprosamples/next-sample-2

These commands will create four sample Deployments with different images.

kubectl get po

Create services

After you have created the Deployments, you will need to create Services for each of them. Run the following commands to create the Services:

kubectl expose deploy sample-1 --type=ClusterIP --port=3000
kubectl expose deploy sample-2 --type=ClusterIP --port=3000
kubectl expose deploy sample-3 --type=ClusterIP --port=3000
kubectl expose deploy sample-4 --type=ClusterIP --port=3000

These commands will create four Services with ClusterIP type for each of the sample Deployments.

Create Ingress resource

Now that you have created the Services, you can create an Ingress resource to route traffic to them based on different paths. To create the Ingress resource, run the following command:

ingress-resource.yaml

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: example-ingress
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
  - hosts:
      - "test.local"
    secretName: tls-secret
  rules:
  - host: "test.local"
    http:
      paths:
      - pathType: Prefix
        path: /sample-1
        backend:
          service:
            name: sample-1
            port:
              number: 3000
      - pathType: Prefix
        path: /sample-2
        backend:
          service:
            name: sample-2
            port:
              number: 3000
      - pathType: Prefix
        path: /sample-3
        backend:
          service:
            name: sample-3
            port:
              number: 3000
      - pathType: Prefix
        path: /sample-4
        backend:
          service:
            name: sample-4
            port:
              number: 3000
kubectl apply -f ingress-resource.yaml

This will create an Ingress resource with rules to route traffic to the sample Services based on different paths.

kubectl get ing
kubectl describe ingress example-ingress

Install certificate manager

If you want to use HTTPS with your Ingress, you will need to install a certificate manager. Run the following command to install the Jetstack cert-manager:

kubectl apply -f https://github.com/jetstack/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.7.1/cert-manager.yaml

This will install the cert-manager as a Deployment in your cluster.

Create Clusterissuer

After you have installed the cert-manager, you can create a Clusterissuer to issue SSL certificates for your Ingress. Run the following commands to create the staging and production Clusterissuers:

prod_issuer.yaml

apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-prod
  namespace: cert-manager
spec:
  acme:
    # The ACME server URL
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    # Email address used for ACME registration
    email: user@gmail.com
    # Name of a secret used to store the ACME account private key
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-prod
    # Enable the HTTP-01 challenge provider
    solvers:
    - http01:
        ingress:
          class: nginx

staging_issuer.yaml

apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
 name: letsencrypt-staging
 namespace: cert-manager
spec:
 acme:
   # The ACME server URL
   server: https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
   # Email address used for ACME registration
   email: user@gmail.com
   # Name of a secret used to store the ACME account private key
   privateKeySecretRef:
     name: letsencrypt-staging
   # Enable the HTTP-01 challenge provider
   solvers:
   - http01:
       ingress:
         class:  nginx
kubectl apply -f staging_issuer.yaml
kubectl apply -f prod_issuer.yaml

These commands will create two Clusterissuers, one for staging and one for production.

Other Commands

Here are some other useful commands to help you manage your Kubernetes cluster:

To view deployments

kubectl get deploy

To view services

kubectl get svc

To view ingress

kubectl get ing

To describe ingress

kubectl describe ing <ing-name>

To view clusterissuer

kubectl get clusterissuer

To view certificate

kubectl get certificate

To describe certificate

kubectl describe certificate

Conclusion:

Ingress is a powerful tool for managing traffic within a Kubernetes cluster, enabling you to route requests efficiently and securely. By leveraging Ingress, you can reduce the complexity of exposing multiple services and simplify your infrastructure. With the NGINX Ingress Controller, you gain robust features for traffic management, including SSL termination and flexible routing rules. Additionally, integrating a certificate manager like Jetstack cert-manager allows you to secure your applications with HTTPS effortlessly. By following the steps outlined, you can set up and configure Ingress to optimize traffic handling and ensure a seamless experience for your users.
